historical_claims.anchor: DNA replication copies genetic material. Chromosome segregation moves copies into different destinations.
This suggests a model called semiconservative replication: each resulting double helix contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.
In 1958, Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl performed an experiment that made those alternatives distinguishable.
After a second generation, they observed both a light band and an intermediate band.
new DNA grows in the five-prime-to-three-prime direction.
Copying is accurate but not flawless.
A typical human diploid somatic cell contains forty-six chromosomes, organized into twenty-three pairs of homologues, before DNA replication.
A surveillance mechanism called the spindle assembly checkpoint helps delay separation when attachment requirements are not satisfied.
During meiosis one, homologous chromosomes pair and are separated from one another.
Gregor Mendel could not see DNA molecules or meiotic spindles.
the genotypes A A, A a, and a a have expected proportions one quarter, one half, and one quarter.
If they lie on the same chromosome, they can be linked and inherited together more often than expected under independence.

description: Connects semiconservative DNA replication and the Meselson–Stahl isotope experiment with proofreading, repair, chromosome segregation and cell division. Contrasts mitosis and meiosis, and explains Mendelian transmission, recombination, linkage and the distinction between DNA damage and inherited mutation.
